name: Liam Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Liam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the yard at Barrow's, the builders' merchant, by six. I drive an 18-tonne flatbed with a crane on the back, so I load plasterboard, timber and blocks, then do four or five drops on building sites around the town. The best bit is swinging a pack of blocks over a fence onto exactly the right spot while the lads cheer. The worst bit is sitting outside a site for forty minutes because nobody booked me in.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, what does life look like at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Nadia, my girlfriend, in a rented flat above the bakery on Mill Road. She's a care worker, so between us we're never flush, and I've got maybe two weeks of money in the bank. My dad drove for forty years and got me into the union the day I passed my test. I'm not a phone person, honestly. The company put a tracking app on my cab tablet last year and I still hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. Every year someone says the robots are coming for drivers and every year I'm still stuck behind a cement mixer on the ring road. I'd say it in the canteen and probably nowhere else, because I don't do social media.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't fix anything for me. My rent went up again in September, and Barrow's has cut the Saturday overtime that used to cover our bills. AI being hype doesn't put money back in my pocket. I'm still one broken boiler away from asking my dad for a loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my rounds and keep my head down. I'd push the union rep to fight for the Saturday shifts back, because that's real money. If I had to, I'd pick up weekend shifts driving for the farm shop's delivery van, but I'd rather not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, more than scared. Being skint all the time wears you down. It's not a disaster, it's just a slow squeeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one broken boiler away. What's the first thing that would go if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably. I share it with Nadia and it's on its last legs anyway. We'd both have to rely on lifts, and she does nights at the care home across town, so that'd be rough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the tracking app that would bother you even in this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, the app scores my braking and my idling and sends it to the office. My manager pulled me up for idling while I was waiting for a forklift that never came. Even dumb software gets used to squeeze drivers.

say: I'd tell the lads in the **canteen** that the robot hype was always nonsense.
I'd keep it **offline**, because I don't post about anything.
think: The real problem is **money**, not AI, because my rent keeps rising and pay doesn't.
Losing the **Saturday overtime** hurt our household more than any machine has so far.
do: Push the **union rep** to win back the Saturday shifts within the year.
Pick up **weekend van work** at the farm shop only if bills force it.
feel: **Tired** and worn down by always being short of money.
S0.quote: AI being hype doesn't put money back in my pocket. I'm still one broken boiler away from asking my dad for a loan.
fieldNote: Liam's worry here comes from **rent** and lost overtime, not from technology.
He already resents the **tracking app** as a tool for squeezing drivers.
His instinct is to lean on the **union** rather than change anything himself.

steps.text: Press the union rep to restore Saturday overtime at the builders' merchant
Keep the same flatbed round and avoid new apps

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office jobs that should worry, not us. Somebody still has to get a pack of plasterboard up a muddy track and lift it over scaffolding. That's what I'd tell anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the thinking side of my job is the bit they'd take first. Planning the drops, booking slots, the paperwork, all that already comes through the tablet. If software plans tighter rounds, they need fewer of us to do the same deliveries. With so few driving jobs round here, being the one let go would be bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union to get it in writing that nobody gets laid off because of new planning software. I'd stop eating out entirely, which isn't much anyway. I'd probably learn the planning screen properly, just enough so the office can't say I'm the slow one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit angry. It's always us at the bottom who have to change how we work, never the people choosing the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the yard would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Pete, who's sixty-one and still does everything on paper. He's slower with the tablet than me, and I'm bad. If they're picking who goes, they'd look at him first and then at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the planning screen. Earlier you said you never touch new tech. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. I don't want to, and I won't go looking for AI stuff. But if the choice is learn the screen or lose the job, I'll learn the screen and moan about it.

say: I'd say the **office jobs** go first and drivers are still needed on site.
I'd point out that **lifting blocks** over scaffolding isn't something software can do.
think: The **planning and booking** side of my job is exactly what software takes first.
Tighter rounds mean **fewer drivers**, and there are hardly any other driving jobs nearby.
do: Ask the **union** for a written no-layoffs promise tied to new software.
Stop **eating out** completely to stretch our thin savings.
Learn the **planning screen** just enough to avoid looking slow.
feel: **Uneasy** about being one of the drivers picked to go.
**Angry** that workers always change while managers choose the software.
S1.quote: If software plans tighter rounds, they need fewer of us to do the same deliveries.
fieldNote: Liam sees that the **thinking parts** of driving, like planning and booking, change first.
He'd learn the screen only under **pressure**, and says so openly.
He worries for **older colleagues** before himself, which fits his union upbringing.

steps.text: Ask the union for a written no-layoffs deal over planning software
Stop eating out and takeaways to stretch the two weeks of savings
Learn the cab tablet's planning screen well enough to keep up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be stopped or slowed down by law. You can't just switch off a whole trade in a few years and leave people with nothing. I'd sign every petition going and I'd say so to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm finished as a driver around 2031, and before that the office will already be run by AI. Two years isn't enough time for someone like me to do anything. I've got no savings, no qualifications past school, and I don't even like using the tablet. I genuinely don't know what I'd be in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. I'd keep driving as long as they let me and go to every union meeting. Maybe Nadia and I would move in with my parents to save rent. Beyond that I can't picture a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, like the floor's gone. I'd lie awake doing the sums. There isn't a version where it works out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Nadia the night you realised that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we might need to give up the flat and go back to my mum and dad's box room. She'd hate it. And her job's caring, so at least there's a chance hers lasts longer than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the robots come about three years after the AGI. Does those three years feel like breathing room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. The trucks might need me till 2031, but the people who decide my hours will be using AI from 2028. I'd spend three years driving and waiting for the letter.

say: I'd demand **laws** that slow automation so whole trades aren't switched off.
I'd sign every **petition** and say it loudly to anyone listening.
think: I expect to be **finished as a driver** around 2031, with the office automated first.
**Two years** gives someone with no savings or qualifications no real chance to prepare.
do: Keep **driving** for as long as Barrow's keeps him on.
Attend every **union meeting** and back any campaign for slower rollout.
Consider moving into his **parents' house** to save rent.
feel: **Sick** and sleepless, with no version of the future that works out.
S2.quote: The trucks might need me till 2031, but the people who decide my hours will be using AI from 2028.
fieldNote: Liam has **no plan** at all here, and admits it plainly.
He sees the three-year **robot gap** as waiting time, not preparation time.
His only levers are the **union** and family, both outside himself.

steps.text: Join union campaigns and petitions for laws slowing driverless trucks
Move with Nadia into his parents' box room to save rent
Keep driving the flatbed until the job is cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said about the fast one: governments need to step in. Five years is still fast, but at least there's time to pass rules about how many trucks can run without a driver. I'd push that in the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me till about 2034 with the truck. It still feels like I'm being pushed off a cliff, just a taller one. I'd be thirty-five, young enough to do something else, but I don't know what, and I'm not good at learning new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting away a bit each month, even fifty, to have something. I'd ask the union about any training they fund, maybe crane operator tickets for bigger cranes, because that's still hands-on. And I'd keep driving until 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but less frozen than with two years. At least I'd have time to argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bigger cranes? Robots come for hands-on work too, around 2034.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know, but tower cranes on big city sites feel like the last thing they'd trust a robot with. It buys a few years, maybe. I'm not saying it's smart, I'm saying it's what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if you're saving fifty a month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Football. I go to the home games with my dad twice a month. I'd have to tell him I'm watching on the telly at the pub instead.

say: I'd say **governments** must set rules on how many driverless trucks can run.
I'd push that **demand** through the union with five years to make the case.
think: I'd have the truck until about **2034**, when I'm thirty-five.
Learning something new scares me because I'm **slow with change**.
do: Save a small **fifty a month**, cutting football tickets to manage it.
Ask the union about funded **crane tickets** for bigger site cranes.
Keep **driving** the flatbed until robots arrive around 2034.
feel: **Scared** but less frozen, because there's time to argue.
S3.quote: Five years gives me till about 2034 with the truck. It still feels like I'm being pushed off a cliff, just a taller one.
fieldNote: Five years turns Liam from **frozen** to slowly moving, but only within what he knows.
His retraining idea, **bigger cranes**, stays close to his current hands-on skill.
Giving up **football with his dad** shows how thin the margin is.

steps.text: Save fifty a month by dropping football tickets with his dad
Ask the union about funded tower crane operator training
Back union calls for limits on driverless trucks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough time to do this properly, with training paid for and nobody thrown on the scrapheap. If they don't use the time, that's a choice the bosses and politicians made. I'd keep saying that at union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and the robots three after that, so roughly 2039. I'd be nearly forty. Part of me thinks I could just ride it out for years. The other part knows that's exactly what my dad did with the mines closing near him, and it didn't end well for his friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably do nothing big in year one, if I'm honest. I'd stay at Barrow's, keep paying union dues, and maybe start the crane ticket in a couple of years. Nadia would push me to do more, and she'd probably be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than scared. It feels far off, which is the problem, because I'll keep putting it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did happen to your dad's friends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few went on the sick and never worked again, one moved away and we lost touch. Dad was lucky he drove. My dad's friends waited too long when the mines near him closed. I don't want to be the one who waited too long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd keep putting it off. What would make you actually move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A date. If the union or the firm said, right, from this year the trunk runs go driverless, I'd sort myself out. Without a date I'll just keep driving.

say: I'd say a **decade** is enough time to train people properly.
If time is wasted, that's a **choice** bosses and politicians made.
think: With robots around **2039**, part of me wants to just ride it out.
My dad's friends who **waited** after the mines closed never recovered.
do: Stay at **Barrow's** and keep paying union dues in the first year.
Start a **crane ticket** in a couple of years, if Nadia pushes him.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than scared, and aware he'll keep **putting it off**.
S4.quote: My dad's friends waited too long when the mines near him closed. I don't want to be the one who waited too long.
fieldNote: Liam knows that a **long runway** tempts him to do nothing.
His dad's memory of **mine closures** shapes how he reads every scenario.
He would act only once someone gives him a **firm date**.

steps.text: Stay on the flatbed round at the builders' merchant for now
Keep paying union dues and attend meetings on driverless plans

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, no question. What would help is someone paying my wages while I train, and a law saying firms can't sack drivers for robots without notice and money. Without that, I'm just hoping.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Nadia. Everyone talks about drivers, but care work is low paid too, and if I go down to nothing she's carrying both of us. I'd want someone to ask what happens to the partners.

headlineQuote: Being skint all the time wears you down. It's not a disaster, it's just a slow squeeze.
portrait: Liam is a **27-year-old** flatbed crane driver at a builders' merchant, with about two weeks of savings.
He rents a flat with his girlfriend Nadia, a **care worker**, and money is always tight.
He trusts the **union** and his father's experience more than technology or employers.
He avoids new tech and has **no plan** when AGI arrives fast.
Longer timelines calm him but tempt him to **put things off**, and he knows it.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years leaves no time or money to change trades.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **training wages** and a law forcing notice and **compensation** before drivers are replaced.
